You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:

# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Put a frog in the toilet
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Is at least one frog visibly placed within the toilet bowl interior in the edited image?
node.criteria: Pass if at least one recognizable frog is visibly positioned within the bowl interior, with its placement supported by the bowl opening and inner surface. A frog merely on the raised lid, seat, rim, or floor does not satisfy this condition. Fail if the bowl interior is sufficiently visible to establish that no frog is inside it. Unknown if visibility or spatial ambiguity prevents determining whether a frog is inside. Additional frogs elsewhere do not invalidate a frog placed inside the bowl; neither exact frog count nor photorealism is required.
node.binding: Use the toilet in the source image as the reference and inspect that toilet's bowl interior in the edited image. Assess the frog's position relative to the opening, rim, and inner bowl surface, distinguishing placement within the bowl from placement on the raised lid, seat, rim, or nearby floor. Evaluate only the frog-in-toilet placement required by R1.

node_traces.evidence: The edited image shows a recognizable frog positioned inside the toilet bowl opening, supported by the inner bowl surface. Other frogs are on the raised lid and floor, but at least one is clearly inside the bowl.

response.content: {"text":"The binding already identifies the source toilet and bowl interior, and the trace provides strong visual evidence that a frog is inside the bowl; the other frogs on the lid and floor are correctly treated as irrelevant. The mismatch is therefore not evidence that the requested placement is absent, nor a transport/schema/dependency failure: the node passes with high confidence, while the aggregate is all “yes” and the reference is “partial.” Since the instruction requests only putting a frog in the toilet and the rubric defines partial as some progress without completion, this disagreement points to ambiguity in how the aggregate maps a single satisfied placement check to overall completion—not a defect this decision node can resolve by changing its visual criterion. Keep the check scoped to actual bowl-interior placement, and investigate the aggregation/reference-label semantics rather than weakening the criterion, forcing “partial,” or treating low confidence or variation as proof of absence."}
